title: Route-aware Adaptive Optimizer: per-customer segmentation, policy allow/deny, and safe apply/rollback
creator: Sofia Ramos
description: Background: As customer workloads differ wildly in traffic patterns and quality sensitivity, a one-size-fits-all auto-batching/caching recommendation risks either under-optimizing for cost or causing regressions in output quality or latency for higher-tier customers. Goal: implement a route-aware adaptive optimizer that (1) segments traffic by customer and route, (2) applies allowlists/denylists and tier-specific policies, (3) provides a dry-run/simulation validation path, and (4) performs safe canaryed applies with automated rollback triggers. This ticket covers the engineering design, implementation plan, and test-run harness to safely apply per-customer/per-route batching & caching config recommendations in production.
acceptance_criteria: Policy model supports selectors for customer_id, route_pattern, model_family, and traffic_tier
Recommendations produced include batching window, max_batch_size, kv_cache_ttl, and cache_scope (global/prefix) per selector
Simulation harness can run recommendations against 7 days of archived traces and report estimated cost delta and predicted latency p95 impact
Safe-apply flow: dry-run -> canary (configured % of traffic) -> staged rollout -> auto-rollback on policy-defined signals
Automated rollback triggers implemented: latency SLO p95 > baseline * 1.15, error-rate spike > baseline + 0.5%, or quality-regression detected by eval set failure rate > 3%
Dashboard surfaces per-customer expected savings, observed delta, cache-hit rate, and rollback events
Unit/integration tests for selector matching, config merge precedence, and rollback signal evaluation
End-to-end test executed in staging with shadow traffic and Canary at 2% for 24 hours with no regressions before scheduling production rollout
technical_notes: Policy schema: list of rules with selector (customer_id|route_regex|model_tag|tier), priority, config_patch, and safety_profile
Config_primitives: batching.window_ms, batching.max_items, caching.kv_ttl_s, caching.scope, quantization_profile (read-only suggestion)
Evaluation engine: replay archived traces with token-level timing model to estimate p95 latency and batching efficiency. Use historical KV hit traces where available to simulate caching benefit.

Safe-apply orchestration: implement in runtime control-plane a state machine: DRY_RUN -> CANARY -> STAGED -> ACTIVE. Each transition requires metric checks or manual approval depending on safety_profile.
Rollback orchestration: automated rollback uses rolling revert with exponential backoff and alerting. Store snapshots of prior config for fast apply (no DB schema changes).
Metric collection: new per-policy tagging on ingested requests so we can attribute cost/latency/quality to policy versions.
Permissions: only ops/release-engineering + policy-owners can schedule global rollouts; product teams can schedule per-customer tests (RBAC enforced).
Backward compatibility: if a selector does not match, we fall back to existing global optimizer; merging respects higher-priority explicit customer rules.
Performance budget: apply path must not add more than 5ms median latency to request routing decision in control-plane path.
rollout_plan: Implement schema + simulation engine in staging (sprint 1)
Integrate metric tagging and validation checks (sprint 1)
Internal alpha: run recommendations as dry-run for 2 weeks across low-risk customers (sprint 2)
Canary apply to 2% of traffic for selected customers with tight monitoring (sprint 3)
Expand to 10% then 50% across segmented tiers if no triggers fire
Full rollout gated by product sign-off and no quality regressions after 7 days
risks: False positives in regression detectors causing unnecessary rollbacks
Selector overlap and priority confusion could lead to unexpected policy application
Simulation mismatch: replay may not capture emergent behaviors (e.g., user prompt distribution change)
Insufficient tagging could make attribution hard, delaying rollback decisions
Ops complexity if many per-customer policies are active simultaneously
